difficultyReason: The principle contains a nested exception clause ('unless … except when'). The correct answer must thread three logical conditions: the general rule, the limiting exception, and the counter-exception that reinstates the rule. Four distractors each stall at a different branch of the conditional chain.
stimulus: A government agency is justified in withholding information from the public only if releasing that information would compromise an ongoing investigation, unless the information concerns potential harm to public health, in which case the agency must release it even if doing so compromises the investigation.
questionStem: Which one of the following judgments most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A regulatory agency declines to release internal audit findings that reveal a widespread contamination risk in the municipal water supply, on the grounds that releasing those findings would interfere with its ongoing inquiry into the source of the contamination.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A law enforcement bureau withholds the identity of a confidential informant from the public because disclosure would compromise an active trafficking investigation, and the withheld information has no bearing on any risk to public health.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A public health department releases detailed case data from a disease outbreak investigation even though it had not yet determined the source, because the agency's director believed transparency would reassure a nervous public.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A food safety office refuses to disclose test results showing elevated toxin levels in a commercial product, citing an ongoing supplier audit, and a court later orders disclosure after the audit concludes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: An environmental bureau releases air-quality monitoring data mid-investigation because a senior official determined that no ongoing inquiry would be meaningfully affected by early disclosure.

explanations.correct: Choice B satisfies all conditions of the principle. The bureau withholds information (the general consequent), the withholding is justified because releasing it would compromise an ongoing investigation (the antecedent), and the counter-exception does not apply because the withheld information poses no public-health risk. Every branch of the conditional is properly navigated.
explanations.A: Violates the principle. The withheld information concerns a contamination risk — a public-health harm — which triggers the counter-exception requiring release even at the cost of the investigation. The agency's refusal to release it is therefore unjustified under the principle, not justified.
explanations.C: Outside the principle's scope and partially inverts it. The principle addresses when withholding is justified; it does not independently authorize or prohibit release. Moreover, the stated reason — reassuring the public — is not among the principle's criteria. This is an 'extra fact misdirection' trap.
explanations.D: Partial fit / violates the principle. The food safety office withholds findings that bear on elevated toxin levels, which constitutes potential public-health harm. The counter-exception requires release; the office's continued withholding is unjustified under the principle regardless of the ongoing audit. Court-ordered post-audit disclosure does not rescue the original withholding.
explanations.E: Outside the principle's scope. The principle governs when withholding is justified; it does not speak to when release is permissible mid-investigation. The scenario describes a release, not a withholding, and the justification given (no meaningful interference) is not a condition the principle addresses.

difficultyReason: The principle has a two-part antecedent plus an 'unless' clause that creates a defeating condition, requiring test-takers to track three logical nodes. Distractors exploit reversed application, partial fit, and a scope error. The correct answer satisfies both positive conditions while the defeating condition is explicitly absent.
stimulus: An architect is professionally obligated to alert a client to a structural deficiency in a proposed design if the architect both identifies the deficiency through reasonable professional inspection and believes the deficiency poses a meaningful risk of injury, unless the client has already been independently informed of the deficiency by a licensed structural engineer.
questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle stated above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An architect notices an unusual load-bearing arrangement during a cursory walkthrough but, having no formal training in structural engineering, decides the assessment falls outside the scope of reasonable professional inspection and says nothing to the client.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An architect conducts a thorough review of building plans and identifies a foundation design that, in the architect's professional judgment, poses a meaningful injury risk; the client's structural engineer has already flagged the same issue in a written report provided to the client. The architect does not raise the issue independently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An architect performing a standard design review identifies a lateral-bracing gap that she believes creates a meaningful risk of collapse under expected wind loads, and no structural engineer has separately advised the client about this deficiency. The architect informs the client immediately.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An architect identifies a cosmetic flaw — an asymmetric facade element — that a structural engineer has not mentioned, concludes it poses no meaningful injury risk, yet alerts the client anyway out of professional thoroughness.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A structural engineer, rather than the project architect, identifies a beam-sizing error that poses a meaningful injury risk and notifies the client; the architect, upon learning of the engineer's report, decides no further action is required on the architect's part.

explanations.correct: Choice C satisfies every node of the principle. The architect identified the deficiency through a standard (reasonable professional) review — first condition met. The architect believes it poses a meaningful risk of collapse — second condition met. No structural engineer has independently informed the client — the defeating 'unless' condition is absent. Therefore the obligation to alert the client is triggered, and the architect fulfills it.
explanations.A: Partial fit / reversed application. The architect declines to act on the grounds that the inspection was not 'reasonable professional inspection.' If that characterization is accepted, the first antecedent condition is not met, so the principle imposes no obligation — the scenario is simply outside the principle's scope. It does not conform to the principle; it describes a case where the principle is silent.
explanations.B: Correctly invokes the defeating 'unless' clause — but this means the principle does NOT obligate the architect to alert the client, so the architect's silence is permissible rather than a conforming application of the obligation. This is a partial-fit trap: test-takers may think the scenario 'conforms' because the architect correctly reads the exception, but conforming to the principle means satisfying the obligation, not merely correctly applying the exception.
explanations.D: Outside the principle's scope. The deficiency is cosmetic, not structural, and the architect explicitly concludes it poses no meaningful injury risk — the second antecedent condition fails. The alert the architect issues is not required by the principle and therefore does not conform to it. This is an 'extra fact misdirection' trap.
explanations.E: Scope error. The principle governs architects' obligations, not structural engineers'. The scenario describes the engineer notifying the client and the architect standing down. Whether the architect's inaction is appropriate is not determinable from this principle, which speaks only to when architects must alert clients — a condition that requires the architect to have identified the deficiency through reasonable professional inspection, which is not established here.
